n is stated (2,416 usable judgments on 400 narratives, 150,000 random stratum), the cell-filling draw and calibration weights are described, and cluster-bootstrap intervals are given on the headline F1, precision and ECE (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4.3, Table 6), and the coder counts reconcile.

The headline REFLEX-Sim success is a task outcome from terminal-state assertions (Sec. 4), but the abstract also reports RF-5C interventions scored against gold actions derived from declared conditions and BFCL accuracy against stored labels (Sec. 4, Sec. 5.4, Table S4), so headline results mix reference types.

n = 100 held-out tasks is stated and paired McNemar and bootstrap results are given for contrasts, but per-condition success intervals for the headline 0.95 are absent ('left blank', Table S14) and how the 100 test tasks were chosen is not described (Sec. 4, Table 1).

Strong-only and REFLEX arms use the identical strong-model configuration including reasoning effort (Sec. 4, Table 4), and tau = 0.5 is stated as the primary operating point with the full threshold sweep reported rather than a best-in-column pick (Sec. 4, Table 1).

The card discloses that Jev figures are third-party published with different sample sizes and prompts, that the 0.766 checkpoint was fine-tuned on the benchmark's own training split, and that Laya's 0.081 ECE comes after temperature fitting (HF card laya, 'Laya (with routing) vs TypeSafe Jev' table and 'Honest Limits' section).

Headline results use verbatim public pre-2026 benchmarks with released answer keys (AG News, DAIR Emotion, Banking77, MASSIVE, XNLI) and no overlap or contamination check is reported (HF card laya, 'Laya (with routing) vs TypeSafe Jev' table and 'Why Route: The Evidence' table).

Section 5.1 text prints 'R1 at tau = 0.5 achieves 95% success with 1.12 calls per task' (first place named, typed without the percent sign); Table 1 row 'R1 tau=0.5' prints 0.95 in the Success column. Read in pdf.txt of arXiv 2609.26532v1.

Several compared rows are served aliases not resolved to a served version (e.g. Liquid AI d1 `d1:free`, `baseten/mammoth-1:free`, meraGPT `sd-1`), the gold teacher is unnamed, and no run dates are given; only Jev carries a full version (1.13.0) (HF card, 'Leaderboard' table and 'Reading a score' section).

Systems differ in training and scoring setup (zero-shot vs fitted or fine-tuned on `train`; scored by the card authors, by HF Jobs or self-reported by creators), but this asymmetry is disclosed and bounded by two separate non-comparable tables, with no report of tuning on test (HF card, 'Leaderboard' table, 'Fitted or fine-tuned on train' table, 'Who scored each row' section).

Headline results mix reference types: accuracy is an LLM-as-a-Judge score against LoCoMo reference answers (judge LLM not named, origin of reference answers not stated), while build time and query latency need no external reference label (Sec. 4.1 'Metrics', Tables 1-2, abstract).

Predictions are scored against the 'existing annotations' of ContractNLI without model-based judging, but the paper does not say how those labels were made (Sec. 2, Limitations, App. C.1), and headline cost and time endpoints need no label.

Sonnet, Haiku and Terra and the four follow-up configurations 'were selected after initial results were inspected' on the same test samples (Sec. 3.1, Limitations), and reasoning budgets also differ across models (App. C.2, App. N).

Sec. 4.1 and Sec. 5 disclose that the combined controller also has improved candidate descriptions and execution handling (catalog 72 vs 73 commands, App. E) and a quantified extra GPT-6 budget (Table 6), a disclosed and bounded asymmetry; two 'local development maps' are in the 35-map result but a 33-map summary without them is reported (Table 3).

Evaluation uses public pre-2026 SMAC-Hard maps and the public AltitudeLE map against built-in AI, seen by the models only through structured observations without answer keys and with no contamination check (Sec. 3.1, Sec. 4.1), which matches 'public items seen only through derived features'.

Appendix A.5 Table 5 pins Jev to 'jev-1.13-20260917' with run date 2026-09-20, but several compared open systems that enter Table 2, Figure 1 and the abstract are listed only by repository name with no revision (e.g. 'jaredpalmer/kev-9b', 'Mapika/decider-0.8b', 'Qwen3-0.6B-Base'), a missing version identifier for the weakest model.

Sec. 3.2 states that the Kimi K2.6 and GLM 5.3 configurations were changed after a first pass on the grid produced empty completions, and Sec. 4.1 states the per-task best LLM is 'selected on the same test items', both settings chosen with feedback from the scored evaluation items (disclosed, with a selection-aware bootstrap in Table 21).

HF card results tables state n per panel (e.g. transfer-v4 locked test 656, breadth-v1 test 3,089), the 'Evaluation' section describes suites and splits, and headline comparisons carry paired 95% bootstrap intervals (2,000 record-level resamples).

Every test decision is labeled with the scenario's designated ground truth for LLM-generated calls (caller MiniMax-Text-01 against scripted secretaries; Sec. 4 'Data', App. B), and the abstract states 'all callers are synthetic', so the reference comes from a synthetic procedure.

Headline endpoints are task outcomes of the harness acting on the target (scenarios hit of 13 seeded vulnerabilities, Table V-VI) and counts/runtime that need no external reference label (Tables VI and VIII, Sec. IX).

The re-test (Table VIII, Sec. IX-C/IX-H) used a harness changed with fixes (salvage step, data-type classifier) chosen after seeing the initial run's failures on the same NimbusCart target, i.e. settings selected with feedback from the scored items, although both arms in Table V had identical parameters.
The @fazxes post says Vercel benchmarked its own fx auto mode (safety) classifier, an internal product task, and names no public benchmark (post text).

The headline 324-example held-out comparison (README, 'Evaluation on 324 held-out examples' table and summary infographic) uses synthetic labels: 'All of the labels are synthetic: a model checked them, and no person has reviewed them' (README, 'Current dataset' section).

Nimble is LoRA-tuned on training data from the same curation pipeline while Jev and the Qwen/Gemma baselines are untuned and run in different precision (README, 'Evaluation on 324 held-out examples' section and its results table), a disclosed difference; the holdout was not used for selection (docs/NIMBLE_TRAINING.md).
The 324 held-out items are new contrastive examples built by the authors and kept family-disjoint from training (README, 'Current dataset' section; docs/NIMBLE_TRAINING.md).

Although the generic question is pre-specified and targeted wording is chosen split-half (Sec. 3.4), the wording comparison uses an in-sample best-of-five generic readout chosen on the evaluation items (Sec. 4.2) and the context results use a best shared question selected on both evaluated versions (Sec. 3.4, Figure 4), i.e. settings selected with feedback from scored items.

Detection instances are new target-model outputs on prompts from public pre-2026 benchmarks, and the human-label sets (HarmBench validation, StrongREJECT human set) are public pre-2026 items, with no contamination check reported (Sec. 3.1, Table 1), a mixture of new items and public pre-2026 sets.

The accuracy, fee-per-correct and completion headline results score against EdgeIntent v1 label tuples that were fixed first by design, with text written by generator LLMs and kept only when an LLM verifier (Claude-Opus-5.5) recovered the tuple (Sec. 4.2), a synthetic procedure; latency needs no reference label.

n is stated (300 test and 60 dev cases per condition, 8,280 in total, Table 3), the generation and sampling design is described (Sec. 4.2-4.3), and 95% case-bootstrap intervals are given on EM and on every headline contrast (Sec. 4.6, Tables 4 and 12); the counts reconcile (23 x 360 = 8,280).

Jev is pinned (typesafe/jev-1.13, responses identify jev-1.13-20260917) with run dates of September 24-25, 2026 for the interpretation layer, but the hosted LLMs are given only as model names (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash) with no revision, and no run dates are given for the RQ5 service-layer runs (Sec. 4.7).

All interpreters share the contract, validator, prompts and caching, but GLM-5.3-Flash runs with reasoning at its lowest setting because no endpoint disables it, a disclosed and bounded budget difference (Sec. 4.7, recorded deviation in Sec. 4.6); dev cases alone were used for prompt checks and threshold calibration (Sec. 4.2).

All judges get the same rubric and output contract and the headline thresholds were frozen on separate selection pairs (Sec. 8, Table 3), but reasoning effort and serving differ across judges and the study states it is not compute-matched, a disclosed and bounded budget difference (Sec. 4, Limitations).

Most headline items are verbatim public pre-2026 benchmarks (RewardBench, JudgeBench, HaluEval, PPE) and the paper says it cannot rule out training exposure (Limitations), so the anchor gives high, but the main results table also includes the authors' new final-answer replies and synthetic controls (Sec. 3, Table 1), and the mixture rule gives unclear.
